title: Bofrot Cake Version
author: Barbara Baeta
desc: Baking powder instead of yeast — coarser and crisper, just as a muffin differs from a slice of bread, and bigger than a golf ball.
longDesc: The modern Ghanaian bofrot, raised with baking powder rather than palm wine or yeast, adapted from a recipe used by Barbara Baeta of Flair Catering in Accra. Six ounces of bread flour has margarine cut into it until the mixture resembles cornmeal, then sugar, nutmeg and baking powder. Egg, milk and vanilla go in all at once with a few swift strokes to keep the batter from becoming tough, and it rests about thirty minutes. The oil goes to 375 and the test is a float: a small amount of dough dropped in will quickly rise to the surface. The balls are usually larger than a golf ball and a little smaller than a tennis ball.
ingredients: 6 oz bread flour — about an 8 fl oz cup of unsifted
1/4 cup evaporated milk plus 1/2 cup water — or 3/4 cup regular milk
5/8 tsp baking powder — a rounded 1/2 tsp
// By a cup she means 8 fluid ounces, not 10.
equipment: Two table knives, or your hands
Deep fryer or deep heavy pan
steps: Sift the flour and salt into a bowl and cut in the margarine, using your hands or 2 table knives, until the mixture resembles cornmeal.
Stir in the sugar, nutmeg and baking powder.
In a separate bowl beat the egg, then add the milk and water, and the vanilla, and mix well.
Make a hole in the centre of the flour mixture and add the liquids all at once, blending with a few swift strokes to keep the batter from becoming tough.
Let the batter sit for about 30 minutes.
While waiting, line a colander with paper towels.

About 10 minutes before the 30 minutes are over, heat the oil in a deep fryer or deep heavy pan to 375 degrees Fahrenheit. Do not fill the pan more than halfway, because the oil will bubble up when the dough is added.
When the oil is hot enough, a small amount of dough dropped in will quickly rise to the surface. If the oil is too hot, the dough will brown too quickly and the centre will not have time to cook.

Slip a soup spoon into the oil to coat it, dip it in the batter, and use a finger or another soup spoon to drop the dough into the oil in the shape of a ball. Make them any size you like, but usually larger than a golf ball and a little smaller than a tennis ball.
If the dough flattens out rather than remaining in the shape of a ball, there is likely too much liquid in the batter.
Cook in batches until they are quite browned on all sides. They will likely turn over as they cook, but use a long-handled slotted spoon to stir and turn them as necessary.
Lift them out into the colander to drain and cool.
Eat them warm or at room temperature.
chefTips: The float test is the oil cue: a small amount of dough dropped in should quickly rise to the surface. No thermometer needed.
A few swift strokes, no more. This is a batter, and over-mixing is what makes a tough bofrot.
Golf ball to tennis ball is the size, and it is bigger than most people make them. The cake version is meant to be substantial.
Flattening rather than holding a ball means too much liquid. Add a spoonful of flour rather than persevering.
Start heating the oil ten minutes before the rest is over, so both are ready together. Her own timing and it is good practice.
Coarser and crisper than the yeast version, just as a muffin differs from a slice of bread. Neither is better — her own verdict is that either way is tasty.
The thirty-minute rest is for hydration, not for rising. Nothing visible happens and the source offers no cue, so the clock is all you have here.
commonMistakes: Dropping batter from a dry spoon.
Skipping the rest, which gives a gritty crumb.
Oil too hot, browning the outside before the centre cooks.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #28B: African doughnut, Cake Version', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Friday 13 November 2009, 12:22 PM. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran'. Quantities, the 30-minute rest, the 375-degree oil temperature and the ball size all confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

ATTRIBUTION, printed on the page and the reason the display author is Barbara Baeta rather than the blogger: 'This recipe is adapted from one used by Barbara Baeta of Flair Catering in Accra.' Baeta is the Ghanaian caterer and cookery authority credited separately in this collection for ayikple and fresh pepper sauce.

Opening lines, verbatim, which identify the post as the companion to the yeast version: 'Today's posting continues yesterday's about the Ghanaian doughnut called bofrot or togbei. Here is the cake version, made with baking powder but not wine and/or yeast.'

Ingredients exactly as printed: '6 ounces of bread flour (about an 8 ounce cup of unsifted)'; '3/8 teaspoon salt (a rounded 1/4 teaspoon)'; '1.5 oz margarine (3 Tablespoons)'; '1.5 oz sugar (3 Tablespoons)'; '1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg'; '1/2 teaspoon vanilla'; '1 egg'; '1/4 cup evaporated milk plus 1/2 cup water (or use 3/4 cup regular milk)'; '5/8 teaspoon (a rounded 1/2 teaspoon) baking powder'; 'vegetable oil for deepfrying'.
THE AUTHOR'S CUP DEFINITION, which governs her weight conversions and is worth keeping: 'Also, remember that by a cup I mean 8 fluid ounces, not 10.'

TWO IMPRECISIONS FLAGGED AND NOT CORRECTED, both being the author's own practical glosses on her fractions: '3/8 teaspoon salt (a rounded 1/4 teaspoon)' — three eighths is nearer a scant half teaspoon; and '5/8 teaspoon (a rounded 1/2 teaspoon) baking powder'. Both the fraction and the gloss are recorded for each. The milk options are internally consistent at 3/4 cup either way.

THE OIL CUES, verbatim: 'When the oil is hot enough, a small amount of dough dropped into the oil will quickly rise to the surface. If the oil is too hot, the dough will brown too quickly and the center will not have time to cook.' THE BATTER CUE, verbatim: 'If the dough flattens out rather remaining in the shape of a ball, there is likely too much liquid in the batter.' THE FAT-RUBBING CUE, verbatim: 'cut in the margarine ... until the mixture resembles cornmeal.' THE FRY-DONENESS CUE, verbatim: 'Cook the doughnuts in batches until they are quite browned on all sides.'

NO FRY TIME IN MINUTES IS PRINTED. A retrieval pass that offered '2-3 minutes per batch' was a fabrication by the summarising layer, caught by the verbatim pass, and is not published. Doneness here is by colour only.

THE REST HAS NO CUE, stated plainly rather than papered over: 'Let the batter sit for about 30 minutes' is time only, with no bubbling, volume, surface or aroma endpoint. This is a chemically leavened batter, not a ferment, so nothing is expected to change visibly and the collection's fermentation rule does not apply — but no cue is invented for it either, and the tips say the clock is all there is.

THE TEXTURE COMPARISON WITH THE YEAST VERSION, verbatim: 'These are faster to make, with a different texture from a yeast version--more coarse and crisp, just as a muffin differs from a regular slice of bread. Either way is tasty.'

THE INGREDIENT DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE TWO VERSIONS, quoted from the page's photo caption and genuinely useful: 'the wine and yeast on the right are the ingredients special to the yeast version, those on the left (the vanilla and margarine) are special to the baking powder version, and all the others are common to both (the sugar, egg, salt, bread flour, nutmeg and baking powder).'
SPELLINGS AND SLIPS AS PRINTED, none corrected: 'farenheit' lower-cased; 'rather remaining' (apparently missing 'than'); 'as the cook' (apparently for 'as they cook').

NO YIELD IS PRINTED. What is printed is a batch-size statement: 'This is a small batch (1/8 of the original recipe, thus some of the awkward measurements).' The six servings above is editorial, and a scaling statement is not stored as a yield.
THE PAIR: this post and the yeast version at GHA114 were published on consecutive days and are explicitly a two-part set.
storage: Best the day they are made. 2 days in an airtight container.
healthBenefits: Bread flour supplies more protein than a soft flour.
Egg and evaporated milk contribute complete protein and calcium.
Faster than the yeast version with no overnight planning.
culturalNote: This is the bofrot most Ghanaians under fifty actually eat — baking powder displaced palm wine the way it displaced sourdough everywhere, and the result is a coarser, crisper, larger doughnut. That it comes through Barbara Baeta's Flair Catering is a reminder that Accra's professional kitchens standardised a lot of what is now treated as home cooking.
